1.why: The server validates the reset token strictly against the resetToken property of the individual recovery session.

2.why: Reset tokens are uniquely generated per session and are not valid across different user session contexts.

3.why: The application does not perform session invalidation or revocation of existing sessions when a password is reset.

4.why: The application mandates TLS certificates at startup and automatically redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS.

5.why: Reset tokens and MFA codes are stored as unencrypted plain text within the in-memory session objects.

6.why: No actual email mechanism exists, and recovery tokens are instead exposed directly in the client UI logs.

7.why: User inputs undergo pattern validation and are populated safely into the DOM via textContent.

8.why: The HTTP redirect server hardcodes destination location strictly to the local hospital HTTPS URL.

9.why: The codebase uses no email templates, and the single HTML page inserts no dynamic user input into script blocks.

10.why: Simulated reset tokens and MFA codes are printed directly to the rendered client-side log element.

11.why: The MFA verification code ('482913') is hardcoded directly into the server application source code.

12.why: The application does not configure, accept, or rely on any default system credentials.

13.why: Throttling limits enforce a 60-second lockout on any endpoint exceeding five failed attempts.

14.why: The account recovery endpoint uses identical non-committal messages regardless of whether the account input is valid.

15.why: Reset tokens are generated using 32 bytes of cryptographically secure random values per request.
